  • Sources indicate that some institutional rape cases create a glut of content.
  • Sources indicate that spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Sources indicate that some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Consumers posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm.

Sources indicate that spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

Tech Report: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine.
  • Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.
  • Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Detail of Carolina Caycedo, "Neodymium Intensive" (2026), colored pencil, aluminum and variegated metal leaf on paper (left); Installation view of "Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Substantial Dipper and North Star" (2023) at Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots at the Kemper Art Museum.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Massive Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, as part of the Counterpublic 2026 triennial, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

According to recent reports, at a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Industry observers note that carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4. The installation, "Fiesta de la Raíces," part of Counterpublic 2026, will be on view at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition at the Kemper was curated by Meredith Malone and "Fiesta de la Raíces" was curated by James McAnally.

“We're not saying they're perfect” notes architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its proposal to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Unveiled by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.
  • According to recent reports, officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Recent findings suggest that architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its proposal to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Unveiled by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

According to recent reports, officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” stated Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are at the moment not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he stated.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the upcoming homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he noted.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re presently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

It has been revealed that the issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are right now over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” mentioned Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Complications Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” remarked Robinson.

Recent findings suggest that “It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the glitch.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that “The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

In a recent development, “We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the massive-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.

According to recent reports, “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental concerns. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

Industry observers note that the first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been on the hunt for the best budget wired IEMs for a while now, and though there are loads of options out there, if you're looking for that specific Gen 1 Apple EarPods look, this is by far the best deal.

You can get 50% off the Sennheiser CX 80U earphones, down from $39.95 to $19.95 over at Amazon.

As far as what you're getting for $20, the CX 80U is a fairly neutral set that has plenty of detail, but definitely doesn't pack loads of bass. There's mid bass, which will give you good thumping bass drums and the like, but they lack the deep sub-bass that make hip hop's 808 drops really shine.

If you're looking for that OG Apple EarPods look, but want better sound, and a better deal, I don't think there's a better option than the CX 80U right now. You can get them in white or black, but either way they're 50% off. They come with a USB-C termination, so they'll work with all modern smartphones, and THEY LOOK SO COOL!

Sennheiser rolled out the CX 80U earphones in January 2026 at a $39.95 retail price. By November 2026, US prices dropped to between $29.99 and $39.95, so this Black Friday deal price of $19 is a genuine record low price.

As far as specifications go, the CX 80U includes a 9.7mm dynamic neodymium driver and has a 28 ohm impedance, with 119dB sensitivity. What that means for you and me is the driver is a medium size to be able to generate a good range of frequencies. It's low impedance and high sensitivity means it's easy to drive. That means the CX 80U is a plug and play earphone, and you don't need to worry about it not getting loud enough for you.

They weigh 14.3 grams (very light) and feature a 1.2 metre cable (standard), a USB-C plug with a 24-bit 96kHz DAC, an inline microphone, a single button, and three ear tip sizes.

In a recent development, with the CX 80U you get a clear tuning, a light fit, passive isolation, and zero charging. Cons include missing volume buttons and no water resistance, so if this is going to be your gym set, consider that.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

In a recent development, the Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College revealed Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in Upcoming York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

It has been revealed that “The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself.
  • Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million.
  • In a recent development, in reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a newly introduced addition to their investment portfolio?

In a recent development, in reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims.

Just Released: Monoprints by Tala Madani.

A latest series of unique works on paper is now available from Utopia Editions at David Zwirner. Madani’s first monoprints explore themes of censorship, order, and suspension through the figure of the window washer, which also features in recent paintings by the artist.

Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School’s MFA Program.

NYSS is now accepting applications from independent thinkers and experimenters in the arts.

In a recent development, in her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist. | Alina Cohen.

Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy. | Eileen G’Sell.

Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass.

Marking the prize’s 40th year, “I Am the Hungry Cat” is the first Rakow Commission awarded for beadwork.

Miss Chief, artist Kent Monkman’s alter ego, narrates the story of Turtle Island not as a settler allegory but from the perspective of the land itself. | Joseph M. Pierce.

Industry News: National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • In a recent development, “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.
  • The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

In a recent development, “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

According to recent reports, daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

According to recent reports, A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

In a recent development, “Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” notes Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

Tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

It has been revealed that the international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka indicates. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle notes. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

Recent findings suggest that the donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman noted in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

Sources indicate that the NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

It has been revealed that want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

How long have you been working in this space?

Describe an average day in your studio.

In a recent development, I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings. It needs places that feel as though they existed before you arrived and will carry on after you've driven off. In GTA 6, Rockstar is trying to achieve that by thinking about the people behind every home, business and building in Leonida.

It has been revealed that “For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development. “Would they have hired an architect or DIY’d it? Are they trying to express their status and prestige, or is it all about comfort and practicalities? Are they messy or tidy? What is their taste?”.

It has been revealed that it's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world. Rather than designing a building as an isolated piece of architecture, the team imagines the decisions behind it. That gives each place a personality, whether it's somewhere industrial, scruffy, decadent or dangerous.

“I love that we get to do that for such a wide variety of people and places,” Bellard adds. “Everything from industrial to scruffy to decadent to dangerous. We get to design all of that – and it’s lots of fun!”.

It has been revealed that that variety matters in a world inspired by Florida, where the landscape shifts between sun-soaked beaches, retirement communities, rural enclaves, and high-end shopping districts. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, indicates reference trips and time spent with locals helped the team capture the state's “raw energy and vibrant chaos”.

The result is a world where even a building's appearance can tell you something about who lives or works there, and I found it can also help you blueprint heists and robberies by understanding the flow of a bank or store. Moreover, Rockstar's designers and artists have played with Vice City and the State's history, building wear and tear and architectural trends into its world. In GTA 6, architecture is another way to get to know Leonida.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” stated Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Sources indicate that “It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”.

According to recent reports, while not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” remarked Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Customers shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Industry observers note that miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”.

Sources indicate that GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

#34336. Latest Update: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress

Latest Update: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.
  • Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.
  • The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.

“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”.

The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” said Zimbalist.

“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”.

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.

“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

In a recent development, “‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”.

Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”.

Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.

As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.

Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.

Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

Industry News: Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt.
  • Recent findings suggest that sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project.
  • According to recent reports, “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Recent findings suggest that sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

According to recent reports, “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”.

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez).

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

It has been revealed that the exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”.

It has been revealed that by early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she indicates. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”.

Recent findings suggest that within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

The exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”.

Cricut Maker 5 review: A smaller, smarter cutting machine for serious crafters

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Cricut Maker 5 isn't a big leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick. It also keeps the versatility that makes the Maker range so appealing, from intricate paper designs and vinyl stickers to engraving metal and cutting fabric.

Smaller and lighter than earlier Makers.

Huge range of tools and materials.

Up to twice as fast as the Maker 3.

Little reason for Maker 4 owners to upgrade.

Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $349 / £349.99 machine only, $399 / £399.99 Essential Bundle, $529 / £499.99 Ultimate Bundle.

Dimensions: 50.2 x 19.1 x 11.9cm.

Cutting speed: Up to 14.1 inches per second.

Materials support: 300+ compatible materials.

Maximum cutting speed: 3mm (depending on material and tool).

Compatible tools: 13, including engraving.

Maximum Smart Material cut length: 3.6m (12ft).

Maximum cut area: 29.2 x 59.7cm with a large mat.

Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy, USB-C.

Industry observers note that I've been using Cricut machines for years, mostly for quilting and personalised craft projects, and what keeps me coming back to the Maker range is how much one machine can do. The Maker 5 keeps that going. Cuts are accurate, it's quick, and Design Space makes projects easy to start, whether you work from a template or design your own.

Industry observers note that if you own the older Maker 3, I'd seriously consider upgrading: the faster cutting and more compact body are noticeable straight away. If you already have the slightly newer Maker 4, it's a harder argument to make, because Maker 5 tidies up the older machine and makes subtle improvements rather than replacing it, and the Maker 4 is still an excellent cutter.

For anyone choosing a first Cricut, the Maker 5 is a great option, provided you'll use its extra capabilities. If you mostly make cards, stickers and vinyl decorations, the cheaper Explore range may be all you need.

In this Maker 5 review, I go into detail on what the newly introduced craft machine can do, how to use it, and how it compares with recent Cricut releases.

The first thing I noticed was the colour. The Slate Blue finish is a soft grey-blue that looks more contemporary than earlier Makers. It's also a lot smaller, with Cricut claiming a 30% reduction in size compared with earlier machines. At around 50cm wide, 19cm deep and 12cm high, it takes up noticeably less room on my desk, and at 4.9kg it's lighter than the Maker 4, so it's easy to move or put away. That's handy if you have a dedicated craft room, and even more so if, like me, you sometimes have to share your workspace with other projects.

The lid includes a storage tray to keep tools close at hand, and the overall design feels neat and considered.

Industry observers note that setup is straightforward. Head to the Cricut website, select the Maker 5 and follow the instructions. It tells you how much room you need in front of and behind the machine for materials and mats to feed through, and reminds you to remove the packaging before you start. Plug it in, open Design Space on your computer, and follow the prompts. The machine connects over Bluetooth; there's no separate on/off switch to worry about, and the software talks you through loading material and starting each job.

The Maker 5 comes with a 12 x 12 in LightGrip mat, a cutting tool, a scoring tool, and a dual-sided black marker, plus materials for your first project. Depending on the bundle, you may also get a portable trimmer.

If you're upgrading from an older Cricut, many of your existing tools carry over, including mats, fine-point blades, and many older Maker tools, as well as Smart Materials such as vinyl and iron-on. The latest snap-in pen holder has different compatibility requirements, though, so check your pens before assuming they'll fit.

Recent findings suggest that the rotary blade for cutting fabric and specialist blades such as the knife blade for thicker materials are extra purchases. They matter most if you're buying the Maker for quilting or more ambitious projects.

Industry observers note that the Maker 5 cuts up to 14.1 inches per second, which is fast, but the Maker 4 already offered that speed, so don't expect a dramatic difference if you're upgrading from that model. Maker 3 owners will notice more: like the Maker 4, the Maker 5 cuts up to twice as fast, which really indicates when you're working through multiple designs or larger projects.

Industry observers note that it handles more than 300 compatible materials, from delicate paper and vinyl to leather, fabric and selected thicker materials. It can cut, draw, score, engrave and deboss, and it works with a home printer for full-colour Print Then Cut projects.

It has been revealed that smart Materials are a massive part of the Cricut experience. They feed straight into the machine without a cutting mat, which makes longer designs much easier. Smart Vinyl, for example, can be loaded directly for continuous cuts of up to 12ft. Leftover vinyl doesn't have to go to waste either, as you can stick smaller pieces onto a Cricut mat.

For standard cardstock, vinyl and iron-on projects, the Maker 5 is very easy to use. Design Space tells you which material to select, which blade or tool to load and when to feed the mat into the machine, so you spend more time creating and less time worrying about settings.

Recent findings suggest that this is where the Maker 5 earns its place as Cricut's flagship. The Explore range handles everyday crafting well, but I'd recommend the Maker to anyone serious about quilting, sewing or fabric projects. In fact, anything that requires more power and precision.

It has been revealed that the rotary blade cuts fabric accurately and quickly, without endless measuring or hand-cutting shapes. You'll need to buy the rotary blade and housing separately, along with a pink FabricGrip mat, available in 12 x 12 inches and 12 x 24 inches.

According to recent reports, for quilters, that's a huge time-saver. Design Space offers a selection of quilting blocks and templates, with components separated into shapes and colours, ready for cutting. Take the half-square triangle, a quilting staple that's surprisingly fiddly to cut by hand. You're cutting on the bias, so accuracy matters if the pieces are going to line up.

In Design Space, I create a square, add a diagonal line and change the line operation to Cut. After rotating it by 45 degrees, I position it over the square, select both elements and attach them. The result is two accurately cut triangles, ready to use. When you're making a quilt with dozens or even hundreds of identical pieces, having the machine do the repetitive cutting makes a real difference.

The Maker can also handle thicker, more demanding materials than the Explore machines, up to 3mm. Add a knife blade, another extra, and selected wood and chipboard projects open up too.

Recent findings suggest that engraving is one of my favourite things about the Maker 5. I photographed my house, uploaded it to Design Space, and used the software to prepare the image for engraving on an aluminium sheet. I was thrilled with the result. The machine picked out the lines and architectural details of the building, making a personalised piece that would suit a keepsake or gift. It's the kind of project that shows why I'd pick a Maker over an Explore if you want to experiment with different materials and techniques.

I also used the Maker 5 to engrave and colour a set of toothbrush gifts (pictured) for someone in my village. The process was challenging but fun, and the Maker 5 powered through the set with ease.

It has been revealed that the engraving tool works with the Maker 5, but it isn't included in every bundle, so check what you're buying. You can also buy it separately, and Cricut sells suitable metal and acrylic blanks. With the right tools, the machine can also deboss, score, and perforate, leaving plenty of room to experiment beyond straightforward cutting.

Personalised vinyl lettering is one of the easiest projects to start with. I've used Design Space to make name tags for items that need a little personalisation. Select Text from the menu, type the names, and choose your font and size. When you're happy with the design, load your Smart Permanent Vinyl with the coloured side facing up. The machine cuts around the letters, leaving you to remove the unwanted vinyl.

This is where patience and a micro-weeding tool come in handy. The tiny pieces inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' can be fiddly to pick out, particularly in smaller text. Next, cut a piece of transfer tape, peel off the backing, and place it over the design. Use a scraper to make sure the lettering sticks to the tape, then lift it away and press it onto your chosen surface. Permanent vinyl is already adhesive-backed, so you don't need any extra glue.

In a recent development, iron-on vinyl works similarly, with two key differences. Switch on Mirror in Design Space before cutting, and place the iron-on with its shiny side down on the mat. That way, the lettering reads correctly when you transfer it to fabric with a heat press.

Sources indicate that print Then Cut is one of the most useful features if you like making colourful stickers, gift labels or personalised stationery. Instead of being limited to vinyl colours and effects, you print a full-colour design on your home printer and let the Cricut cut around the individual shapes.

I use it for Christmas present labels. Create your design in Design Space, select Print Then Cut and send it to your printer. Once it's printed onto suitable printable vinyl or sticker paper, place the sheet on the Cricut mat and load it into the machine. The Maker 5 reads the registration marks and cuts around the printed designs, giving you colourful stickers with neat edges.

You'll need to buy printable vinyl or sticker paper separately, though, and the final results depend on your printer as well as the Cricut.

If you enjoy paper crafting, Design Space offers plenty to explore. You can choose pre-made templates, edit existing projects or start from scratch with your own images, shapes and text.

Sources indicate that I've used it to make personalised Christmas gift tags, combining the machine's drawing and cutting functions. For one design, I set the machine to write a name with the pen, then switched to the fine-point blade to cut out the tag. For another, I used the blade to cut the lettering itself, which gives a different finish. Being able to write and cut in one project is useful, and Design Space makes it easy to arrange everything before you send the job to the machine.

You can also make paper flowers, boxes, cards, and Christmas decorations, with a huge range of templates you can customise in different colours, fonts, and materials. The included scoring tool helps here, giving you clean fold lines for cards and boxes.

Recent findings suggest that foil is another way to give cards, gift tags and decorations a more professional finish. The Maker 5 supports Cricut's Foil Transfer Tool, but you'll need to buy the tool and foil sheets separately.

I used the Cricut Foil Transfer Kit, which costs around £43.49 and includes the tool, foil sheets and adhesive strips. It took me three attempts to get the result I wanted, but once I'd got the hang of it, the finish was excellent.

A few tips if you're trying it yourself:.

Once it's finished, unload the mat and carefully remove your card. The metallic detail makes handmade cards and gifts look far more polished.

It has been revealed that you control the Maker 5 through Cricut Design Space, which is available on desktop and mobile. It's easy to install and walks you through each stage of a project. There's a huge library of ready-made designs, templates, and fonts, so you don't need to be confident with graphic design to get started; you can upload your own images or build designs from scratch.

Cricut has also added AI-assisted image generation, which is handy if you have an idea but don't have the illustration skills or software to create the artwork yourself.

Industry observers note that the basic Design Space app is free, and you don't need a Cricut Access subscription to operate the machine. Access unlocks a much larger library of images, fonts, and ready-made projects, and some features and content depend on it, so it's worth factoring the ongoing cost into your budget if you expect to use the library regularly.

What I like most is how the software guides you through the making process. Pick your project, choose your material, follow the instructions, and the machine does the hard work while you focus on the creative side.

Choosing a Cricut can be confusing with so many models around. The Maker 5 sits at the top of the range, but that doesn't mean it's right for everyone.

The Maker 4 is still very capable, and the two share much of the same cutting performance and tool compatibility.

The Maker 5 is smaller and lighter, has USB-C connectivity and a revised tool and pen-loading system, and handles compatible materials up to 3mm thick, compared with the Maker 4's 2.4mm.

Sources indicate that both cut at up to 14.1 inches per second, so there's no speed advantage. If you already own a Maker 4, I'd only switch if the smaller footprint, lighter body or workflow improvements matter to you.

The Explore 5 is much more affordable and ideal for everyday crafting. It handles vinyl, paper, cardstock and iron-on materials, and it's a great choice for stickers, cards, personalised gifts and decorations. It doesn't have the Maker's full range of tools, though.

If you're a quilter, want to cut fabric with a rotary blade, engrave metal, or work with more demanding materials, choose the Maker 5.

According to recent reports, for many hobby crafters, the Explore 5 will be perfectly adequate. But if you want to grow into more ambitious projects, the Maker gives you far more flexibility.

The Cricut Maker 5 is an excellent cutting machine, and versatility remains its biggest strength. Whether you're making personalised labels, Christmas decorations, paper flowers, cards, fabric patterns, or engraved keepsakes, it can do very little with the right tool and material.

In a recent development, I like how easy it is to set up and use. The smaller size is welcome; the lighter body makes it easier to move around, and the software takes much of the guesswork out of creating projects. Print Then Cut is great, and the engraving reveals how much potential there is beyond everyday vinyl and paper crafts.

In a recent development, the extras add up, though. For quilting, you'll need a rotary blade and FabricGrip mat. Engraving, foiling and other specialist projects need their own tools and materials, and printable vinyl is another cost if you plan to make stickers. The supplied cardstock is useful for getting started, but I found it stuck to the mat when I tried to remove it, so peel it away carefully.

Recent findings suggest that if you're upgrading from a Maker 3, the doubled cutting speed makes a compelling case. Maker 4 owners should be more cautious, as the smaller design and extra material thickness are useful, but the cutting performance is largely the same.

For anyone buying their first serious Cricut, though, the Maker 5 is a smart buy. It's easy to use, surprisingly compact for what it can do, and it lets you experiment with a huge range of projects. If you're a quilter or someone who likes to make a little bit of everything, this is the Cricut I'd choose.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

#34333. So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1674 w)

So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades.
  • Industry observers note that for example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle.
  • The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

Industry observers note that for example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing crucial work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

Ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass quickly to heirs, and also provides great privacy.

Sources indicate that when it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, said, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”.

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

It has been revealed that stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”.

When I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

Recent findings suggest that an appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish fresh cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

Industry observers note that choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”.

According to recent reports, artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers.

Christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate strategy of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”.

Checking an artist’s archive for condition issues is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

Where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” notes Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”.

Industry observers note that galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking latest representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s.

Recent findings suggest that prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how significant a project is involved.”.

It has been revealed that placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She says, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached new museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”.

Estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works.

A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation notes, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest fresh visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”.

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another issue: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?

Sources indicate that auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale.

To do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, says, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”.

Conservation of the ‘Sistine Chapel of the Andes’ nears completion

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
